name: Ice-cold face baths

lead: An ice-cold face bath means submerging the face in a bowl of cold or iced water for short intervals. People use it in the morning to reduce a puffy, flushed look, and it has been widely discussed on social media and in beauty coverage.

The proposed chain is simple: cold constricts blood vessels, which can briefly reduce swelling and redness, so the face looks less puffy for a few hours. Dermatologists quoted in the press describe it as short-term symptom control and say there is no strong evidence of lasting skin changes.

paras: In the routines described in beauty coverage, people fill a bowl with cold water and ice and hold the face in for brief dunks of seconds at a time, repeated a few times, usually in the morning or after a workout. Cold rollers and chilled tools are described as a similar, less intense alternative.

Dermatologists say extreme cold can worsen redness, trigger flares and compromise the skin barrier, and that prolonged ice contact can cause discoloration or a cold burn. People with sensitive skin, rosacea, broken capillaries, eczema, cold-triggered hives or recent cosmetic procedures are told to avoid it or take care. Cold-water facial immersion also triggers the diving reflex, which slows the heart rate.

web.title: Is dunking your face in ice water really beneficial? Derms weigh in (NBC News Select)

chain: Temporary reduction in swelling and redness
Face looks less puffy for a few hours
angle.text: The cold narrows blood vessels in the skin, which can briefly flatten puffiness around the eyes and cheeks and calm flushing. People use it as a quick morning or post-workout step.

lead: Ice-cold face baths, also called ice water facials or face dunks, are a routine in which the face is briefly immersed in cold or iced water. They are used to reduce morning puffiness and redness and to give the skin a refreshed look, and they have circulated widely in skincare media.[1]

Dermatologists quoted by NBC News describe the effect as temporary: Dr. Anetta Reszko says cold can temporarily reduce inflammation, puffiness and redness, while Dr. Shamsa Kanwal calls the main value short-term symptom control, such as morning puffiness or post-workout flushing.[1]

Physiology literature on cold-water face immersion concerns the mammalian diving reflex rather than skincare: wetting and cooling the face slows the heart by roughly 10 to 25 percent and constricts blood vessels in the limbs and organs.[2]

paras: The routine is described in beauty and dermatology coverage as short dunks in a bowl of ice water, usually repeated for a total of under a minute, followed by normal skincare.[1] Puffiness is usually attributed by dermatologists to fluid retention linked to salt and alcohol intake, allergies and poor sleep, which cold treatment does not address.[1]

Dr. Kanwal says there is no strong evidence that regular facial ice baths create lasting anti-aging changes such as boosting collagen.[1] Dr. Reszko says extreme cold can worsen redness, trigger flares and compromise the skin barrier, and advises that people recently treated with cosmetic or dermatologic procedures avoid ice baths until the skin has recovered.[1]

The physiology of cold-water facial contact is described in reviews of the diving reflex: wetting and cooling the nostrils and face while holding the breath slows the heart, with the effect growing as water temperature drops, and irregular heartbeats are common during breath-hold dives.[2]

Dermatologists named in coverage advise stopping immediately when pain, burning, numbness, dizziness or a headache occurs.[1] People with sensitive skin, rosacea, broken capillaries, eczema or chronic inflammatory skin conditions are advised to avoid it or use extreme caution.[1]

No studies found on facial ice baths for puffiness or skin appearance. Related physiological research concerns the diving reflex, in which facial cooling slows the heart rate and constricts blood vessels.[2]
